title: adaLN-Zero block
goal:
Implement the adaLN-Zero DiT block (Section 3.2, Figure 3). A linear layer regresses six vectors from the conditioning vector $c$ (the sum of the timestep and class embeddings): $\gamma_1, \beta_1, \alpha_1$ for the attention half and $\gamma_2, \beta_2, \alpha_2$ for the MLP half. Each half computes $x \leftarrow x + \alpha \odot F(\mathrm{LN}(x) \odot (1 + \gamma) + \beta)$.

Write `modulate(h, shift, scale)` and `dit_block(x, c, W, b, attn, mlp)`. `x` has shape `(T, d)`, `c` has shape `(d,)`, `W` has shape `(d, 6*d)`, and `b` has shape `(6*d,)`. Split `c @ W + b` into six chunks in the order `shift_attn, scale_attn, gate_attn, shift_mlp, scale_mlp, gate_mlp` (this is the order of the authors' released code; the paper doesn't fix it). `LN` has no learned affine part and uses `eps = 1e-6`. The same six vectors apply to every token.

With `W = 0` and `b = 0`, the block must return `x` exactly.
hints: `layer_norm(x)` normalizes over the last axis. It is finished for you.
`modulate(h, shift, scale)` is `h * (1 + scale) + shift`. The `1 +` is what makes zero parameters leave the normalized value unchanged.
`np.split(c @ W + b, 6)` returns the six chunks. Each has shape `(d,)` and broadcasts over the token axis.
The gate multiplies the sub-layer output before the residual add: `x = x + gate * attn(h)`. Gating the sum `x + attn(h)` is a different function.
